article.title: Stella Lefty: Data Center Music
article.author: Nikil Soto
article.content: When Stella Lefty wrote the chorus to “Boston,” she was waiting in Nashville for a boy from outside Atlanta. Why Boston? She had a gig coming up there, she told Taste of Country . A month later she noticed it was also the name on the piano. Lefty posted the chorus on TikTok before there were verses to go with it. “Boston,” the breakout single from her debut album, Long Way Home , reached number two on the Billboard Hot 100 and number one on country radio. Try saying “I like it when you’re nice to me” aloud. Now hear how her bright, raspy voice tumbles into it over the acoustic guitar , pleased and a little embarrassed at what she’s admitted. Two verses would seem ample opportunity to give us one example of the guy being nice. Much of the case against Lefty rests on her birth certificate. Born Stella Lefkofsky, she grew up in Glencoe , on Chicago’s North Shore, went to Tulane University, and moved to Los Angeles. Her father, Eric Lefkofsky, cofounded Groupon and runs the health tech company Tempus AI. A billionaire’s daughter singing in a Southern accent about boys in pickup trucks was always going to take some grief. What’s worth resenting is how few of the people who build those pickups can afford to give their kids a few years to find out whether they’ve got a song in them. Give somebody an instrument and years to get good at it without having to earn a living, and now and then you get Gram Parsons . The grandson of a Florida citrus magnate, Parsons could sing about the riches he’d enjoyed and make you feel how badly he wanted to be up in a South Carolina oak tree again. Lefty put her own advantage nicely when she told Vanity Fair , “I didn’t have a stopwatch.” Country owes a great deal to people who worked by the clock for a wage. Southern millhands played some of its earliest dance music. Jimmie Rodgers learned from the black crews he worked alongside on the railroad. Even Trisha Yearwood’s gloriously juvenile “ She’s in Love With the Boy ” turns on what a boy can afford. Tommy proposes outside the Tastee-Freez with his high school ring. When Katie’s father objects, her mother reminds him what a catch he was as a penniless farm boy. By the last chorus, you’ve met four people and taken sides in a family fight. On Long Way Home , you can spend fourteen songs trying to get to know two people that well. In “ Whiskey ,” Lefty is so taken with the way a man talks that she’s struck dumb. We learn roughly as much about him as the bartender does — he likes his drinks on the rocks. I prefer “ Missing You ,” where she’s already nostalgic for the relationship while she’s still at his place wearing his T-shirt. He’s one door away. It’s funny and a little mortifying, which is how a person in love occasionally ought to sound. The plagiarism complaints are harder to shrug off. In “Boston,” you can hear the little hop in the melody of Noah Kahan’s “Stick Season,” right down to the way the singer comes back and does it again on the next line. It’s the only part of “Boston” you can hum to. Lefty told Vanity Fair she hadn’t been thinking about Kahan when she wrote it. She had, however, covered “Stick Season” on TikTok. Kahan got a writing credit after his team flagged the resemblance, shortly before the single came out. “Summer You Were Mine” deliberately borrows from the Chicks’ “There’s Your Trouble.” Rolling Stone verified that the interpolation was cleared before release. The original writers, Tia Sillers and Mark Selby, get their due. The tune fares worse. In the Chicks’ song , a woman has to explain to a lovesick man that the right girl is standing here talking to him. In Lefty’s song, what came between the lovers was September . Listeners heard Blake Shelton’s “ I’ll Name the Dogs ” in the album closer, “ Why Wouldn’t We .” Both choruses itemize what each partner brings to the relationship. Lefty has at least reassigned the job of telling the jokes. In October, after Lefty played an unreleased song called “Badly” at Nashville’s Bluebird Cafe, Shaylen and TAELA put it side by side with their own “WATCH THIS.” TAELA singled out the vocal phrasing and cadence. Allow for coincidence, unconscious imitation, and every last one of the credits, and you still have a debut filled with hooks from somebody else’s back catalog. That’s a poor return on fourteen chances to introduce yourself. There’s no need to believe in castigating people for their inherited privilege, but they should at least take advantage of all the time and security it affords. What explains Stella Lefty’s sudden rise, then? By August, the trade publication Hits was touting more than half a million videos using “Boston.” It had the feeling to many of an “op.” But the kids singing every word at CMA Fest settle the question of whether Lefty has real fans. Labels pay for clips that look like ordinary recommendations and have long helped manufacture demand for their artists. How much of that happened here, if any, remains an open question. You can forgive a listener a little skepticism the fifth time her phone invites her to discover a billionaire’s daughter. Lefty and her team tested takes on TikTok to see which songs to pursue, according to Crain’s Chicago Business . Once “Boston” took off, her label moved the album’s release from September to August . Here was a young woman with the means to take as much time as she liked, suddenly rushing to finish a record. Turns out somebody did have a stopwatch. Take “Something to Lose,” her duet with Vincent Mason. Their voices fit beautifully together. On the record, they meet at 2 in the morning in “a Southern state.” In life, they met at Schulman’s in East Nashville. She brought three friends as chaperones. Her producer remembers drinking Chartreuse. Her cowriter Grace Enger got a burger inside while Lefty and Mason flirted outside. All those songwriters at the bar, and somehow the burger and the Chartreuse didn’t make the cut. For all I know, the person who poured that Chartreuse has a worse country record in them than Stella Lefty. I’d happily run the risk of hearing it. A billionaire’s daughter gets the time off first and a chance to find out how good she is. The results turned out to be derivative and mediocre.
